title: A Room for the House
premise: Mirabel Fairweather, an urban explorer who documents abandoned places as a form of devotion, discovers a network of tunnels beneath her hometown that appear on no survey—except in the ledgers of the town's founding families, including her own. Waiting on her late grandmother's porch is Wren, the imaginary friend she outgrew at nine, unchanged and increasingly desperate. Mirabel learns the founders bound something beneath the town using a ritual of names and rooms, and that her family's inheritance includes the obligation to finish what they started before the binding fails. In the end, Mirabel chooses to give the thing below not a prison but a room—a place inside the house of the living—completing the founders' work as mercy rather than captivity, with Wren as witness and the found family of tunnel-dwellers as her new kin.
about_author: Coral Ishikawa is a former municipal archivist who spent a decade cataloguing property records for towns that no longer exist. She writes horror about paperwork, inheritance, and the things families agree never to mention.

chapters.title: The Survey That Isn't
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Documenting a collapsed storm drain, she finds hand-carved thresholds and a ledger bearing her grandmother's name listing rooms that match no building. The emotional beat is the thrill of discovery curdling into recognition: someone in her family knew. She photographs everything, because documentation is a kind of prayer—and the flash reveals footprints behind her that end mid-stride.

chapters.title: Wren on the Porch
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Her childhood imaginary friend sits waiting on the porch of the inherited house, adult-sized now but wearing the same face, insisting he kept the promise to wait. Through his fragmented memories and the ledger, she learns the founders' ritual: four rooms, four names, one left unfinished. The beat is dread braided with tenderness—Wren is terrifying and the only company she trusts.

chapters.title: What the Founders Owed
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, intercut with ledger entries. Descending with the tunnel-dwellers—squatters who've become an accidental congregation guarding the thresholds—she reaches the fourth room and meets the bound thing: not a monster but the founders' dispossessed partner, erased from every record. The beat is fury and grief; justice was never written into the deed. Time collapses as the binding begins failing around them.

chapters.title: A Room for the House
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. As the tunnels flood with the unbound thing's grief, Mirabel performs the final rite differently: she enters its name into the ledger, carves it a threshold above ground, and offers it a room in the living house instead of a cell. Wren holds the door; the dwellers hold the line. The beat is costly peace—the town keeps its shape, Mirabel gains a family, and some inheritances are meant to be rewritten.
